title_original: Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother review – Mahershala Ali’s religious hitman on the hunt for baby milk

blocks.text: T here are shades of John Woo and Tarantino here in a black-comic thriller from Pakistani-American director Bassam Tariq. There are shades also of Blade, the Marvel character that this film’s star, Mahershala Ali, had been preparing to play in a planned but then cancelled MCU movie which Tariq was going to direct. Here Ali plays Latif, a military veteran turned hitman for hire who uses knives and swords, not guns, and just happens to be a devout Muslim. The title refers to the Islamic tradition in which Muhammad was asked three times who is the most deserving of respect and replied each time: “Your mother.” It is, however, this film’s semi-intentional irony that mothers and female authority figures are largely irrelevant in it, the drama being more about men without women.

blocks.text: Latif is just finishing off a chaotic wet job in a squalid public bathroom one day, when he takes a call on his mobile from his teenage daughter Fatiha (played by Adia, from Steven Soderbergh’s streaming series Full Circle) telling him that his wife, Fatiha’s mother, has died. Convulsed with guilt at having neglected the family home for his homicidal profession, Latif arrives back to find his son Qadir (Jahleel Kamara) acting out, and his newborn baby allergic to formula, and only able to drink the expressed breast milk of which his late wife has left a limited stockpile in the fridge. So now this tough guy has to put the baby in a papoose and go around getting breast milk from Muslim family charities.

But his uncaring mob-boss minder Mike (Laith Nakli) is furious with him for turning down his latest commission: whacking a fundamentalist Christian pastor (John Cho) who wants to take righteous vengeance on Mike’s creepy nephew Hatty (Abubakr Ali), a loathsome young man presiding over a grotesque Hefner-style mansion where Muslim-themed porn is being produced.

The movie is boisterous and frenetic, well acted by Ali and everyone else and interestingly shot in dense, saturated colour by cinematographer Katelin Arizmendi. It is flavoured with irony, although given that we are clearly supposed, at some level, to take Latif’s religious convictions seriously, the film doesn’t quite resolve the irony of a devout Muslim being a paid killer.
